opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a milestone because it changes what the bottleneck is.

For most of the history of deep learning, progress depended on humans: humans collecting data, labeling it, designing the reward, deciding what the model should learn next. Even with large-scale pretraining, we were basically compressing what humanity had already written down. That's incredibly powerful, but it has a ceiling. At some point you run out of high-quality human data, and you can't really exceed the quality of the signal you're imitating.

When a model can start to train itself, by generating its own tasks, attempting them, checking whether it succeeded, and learning from that, the loop no longer has a human in every step. In domains like math and code, where you can verify an answer, we've already seen that reinforcement learning lets models discover reasoning behaviors nobody explicitly taught them: going back to check their work, trying another approach, spending more thought on harder problems. To me that was a very striking moment, because it showed the model wasn't just copying patterns. It was finding strategies through its own interaction with the problem.

So the milestone isn't that the model gets a few points better on a benchmark. It's that the source of improvement shifts from "how much data humans can give it" to "how much compute and how good an environment we can build for it." That's a fundamentally different scaling regime. It's closer to how AlphaGo went beyond human play: once the system could play against itself, human games were no longer the limit.

Of course, we're still early. Self-training works best where there's a clear verifier. For open-ended things like writing, research taste, or real-world agent tasks, defining what "good" means is still hard, and there's real risk of the model gaming its own reward. But I think the direction is clear. The labs and researchers who figure out how to build rich environments and reliable feedback signals will be the ones who push intelligence forward. That's why I see it as a turning point rather than just another technique.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a milestone because, until very recently, every step in the loop of making a model better has had a human somewhere in it. Humans decide what data to collect, humans label it, humans write the reward signals, humans look at the failures and say "this is wrong, go fix it." The model itself is the object being trained. It's passive.

What's changing now is that the model is starting to become the subject in that loop. It can generate its own training data. It can judge whether an answer is good or bad. It can look at its own mistakes and produce a corrected version, and then that corrected version becomes the next round of training signal. Once you close that loop, the limiting factor is no longer how many annotators you can hire or how fast your researchers can read logs. The limiting factor becomes compute and the quality of the verification signal.

And that's a qualitative change, not just a quantitative one. Historically, the bottleneck of AI progress was human knowledge: we could only teach a model what we already knew how to label. Self-training means the model can, in principle, go beyond the frontier of the people who built it, the same way AlphaGo did in Go. Go was easy because the rules give you a perfect verifier. The open question for language models is how far you can push that in domains where the "rules" are fuzzier, like math and code first, then science, then maybe general reasoning.

So when I call it a milestone, I don't mean that the problem is solved. I mean we've crossed the point where the model participates in its own improvement, and from here, progress starts compounding in a way that doesn't depend on us keeping pace.

astra-6.text:
I see it as a milestone because it changes what limits AI’s progress. Today, people still do much of the work: we prepare data, design training methods, evaluate results, and decide what to improve. If an AI can take on more of that cycle—identify its weaknesses, create useful training problems, and learn from feedback—it can improve with less human intervention at each step.

But generating its own data isn’t enough. The crucial question is whether it can reliably distinguish a real improvement from a mistake it has simply reinforced. That requires feedback we can trust.

So, for me, the milestone is closing that learning loop. It doesn’t mean the system suddenly becomes infinitely capable. It means AI starts participating in the process of advancing its own capabilities, and that could significantly change the pace of progress.

sol-6.1.text:
Because it changes how AI improves. Until now, progress has depended heavily on people preparing data, labeling examples, and telling models what a good answer looks like. If a model can generate useful training problems, evaluate its own attempts, and learn from that feedback, it can take on part of that work itself.

The important distinction is between producing more data and producing a reliable learning signal. A model can repeat its own mistakes, too. But when it can test an answer—for example, by running code—it has a way to discover something beyond simply imitating its training data. That creates the possibility of a cycle where greater capability helps produce better training, which then leads to greater capability. That’s why I see it as a milestone.
